How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Engaging in short periods of wakeful rest following encoding can benefit later memory retrieval of encoded material. The magnitude of and mechanisms driving this wakeful rest effect are, however, unclear. Accordingly, this review's main objectives are 1) estimating an aggregate wakeful rest effect, 2) identifying the main experimental determinants of the wakeful rest effect, and 3) synthesizing insights on the mechanisms driving the wakeful rest effect. For this preregistered meta-analysis (PROSPERO registration number CRD42023487595), we searched Google Scholar, PubMed, PsycInfo, PsycArticles, and Web of Science for all peer-reviewed studies of adult healthy and memory-impaired humans, manipulating participants' post-encoding activities to compare declarative memory performance between periods of wakeful rest and other activities. Final update searches were conducted on 29.09.2026. The identified studies were assessed for potential risk of bias using the RoB 2 tool and synthesized in a three-level metaregression approach. In total, we included 55 studies with 4005 individual participants contributing data. An aggregate wakeful rest effect of g = 0.35 (95% CI [0.23, 0.46], p < .001) was found, indicating better memory performance following post-encoding rest compared to active comparator conditions. Our results show that the magnitude of the wakeful rest effect is associated with several, partially intercorrelated, experimental characteristics, including population, comparator condition, and memory measure, and reveal a clear pattern: human declarative memory performance benefits from post-encoding wakeful rest when demands on our memory system are particularly high.

1 Introduction

Brief periods of wakeful rest following encoding are thought to benefit declarative memory performance by facilitating consolidation. Numerous studies compare memory performance regarding previously encoded material between post-encoding intervals of either wakeful rest or a cognitively demanding comparator condition (e.g., Cowan et al., 2004; Dewar et al., 2007; Mercer, 2015; Varma et al., 2017; Scalia & Wamsley, 2026). In these studies, all employing a similar basic paradigm (see Fig. 1), researchers often observe better memory performance following the wakeful rest condition. While this is generally seen as a consequence of consolidation processes (see Wamsley, 2022), this interpretation relies on indirect evidence, and careful consideration of alternative accounts and their applicability to the available data is needed to derive a clearer understanding of the wakeful rest effect specifically and human memory function generally.

Fig. 1. Typical wakeful rest paradigm. Participants are presented with memory material, e.g., a word list or a story (encoding), and immediately afterwards are optionally probed regarding retention (immediate retrieval). Then the critical manipulation takes place during the subsequent delay interval, and participants are either asked to rest (wakeful rest condition) or engage in demanding tasks (comparator condition). A washout period in which participants from both conditions do an identical task for a few minutes can follow. Finally, retention regarding the initially presented memory material is probed (delayed retrieval).

Since the earliest investigations into comparable memory processes by Müller & Pilzecker (1900), various explanations for the wakeful rest effect have been put forward. In the following, we will focus on the two most prominent accounts, increased Trace Consolidation and reduced Trace Competition during rest, which subsume several related ideas.

The Trace Consolidation account explains the wakeful rest effect as a result of variable consolidation of memory traces. Specific neural processes like memory reactivation and memory replay (Dudai et al., 2015) strengthen or consolidate initially weak memory traces. These processes occur primarily opportunistically during periods of rest when encoding demands are low (Wixted, 2004; Mednick et al., 2011). Periods of wakeful rest thus allow for more consolidation of the memory traces than active comparator conditions, which ultimately facilitates retrieval (Dewar et al., 2007). This account assumes consolidation to work via longterm potentiation-like processes, which strengthen synaptic connections between neuronal populations recruited into the engram, the total physical substrate of the memory trace, at the time of encoding (Josselyn et al., 2015). A schematic illustration of how this mechanism is implemented on the engram level is depicted in Fig. 2. Orange coloration indicates recruitment of the neural ensemble to the to-be-remembered engram. Yellow coloration indicates activation of an ensemble at the time of retrieval via a retrieval cue. Memory traces are initially fragile following encoding. During rest, they are consolidated. Retrieval cues lead to more complete reinstatement in better-consolidated traces. Retrieval failure caused by interference is insufficient reinstatement as a consequence of reduced trace consolidation.

Besides explaining the wakeful rest effect, several pieces of evidence support the Trace Consolidation account. Consolidation mechanisms have been observed in humans (Deuker et al., 2013) and non-human animals (Foster & Wilson, 2006) during wakeful rest and are causally linked to memory performance (Ego-Stengel & Wilson, 2010). Craig et al. (2018) have even shown that brief periods of rest facilitate knowledge generation, which has been interpreted as evidence of systems consolidation. However, there are closely related memory phenomena occurring at similar time scales that the Trace Consolidation account cannot readily explain. Proactive interference, a reduction in memory performance due to experiences preceding encoding of the relevant memory material, cannot be explained by a mechanism acting after encoding. Primacy effects are difficult to reconcile with the Trace Consolidation account, as the presentation of additional material following the first memory items should interfere with their consolidation. Furthermore, there is abundant evidence for similarity-based retroactive interference in A-B, A-C list-learning paradigms (reviewed by Wixted, 2004), which is in opposition to the unspecific encoding demands assumed to drive interference with consolidation.

An alternative mechanism, which we will refer to as the reduced Trace Competition account, explains the wakeful rest effect as a result of variable competition among memory traces. This account subsumes several related ideas, including protection from interference (Wamsley, 2022), cue-overload (Wixted, 2004), and temporal distinctiveness (Brown et al., 2007a , Brown et al., 2007b). Within the reduced Trace Competition account, reduced encoding of competing memory traces during wakeful rest compared with the comparator conditions leads to memory traces being more distinct and easier to retrieve, increasing memory performance (e.g., Neath & Brown, 2006; Ecker et al., 2015a; Ecker et al., 2015b). This mechanism explains the wakeful rest effect, proactive interference, primacy effects, and similarity-based retroactive interference. By viewing temporal context as a key feature in causing trace overlap, this mechanism can also explain the temporal gradient of retroactive interference (Ecker et al., 2015a) as well as unspecific retroactive interference caused by interfering material dissimilar but presented in close temporal proximity to the previously encoded material. With respect to its neurobiological underpinnings, this account can be explained as an overlapping recruitment of neuronal populations into the relevant engrams. This is consistent with the idea of neuronal competition in engram formation, as transient changes in excitability of engram-forming neuronal populations facilitate further recruitment of the same excitable populations into new engrams, which results in trace overlap between memory traces encoded in close temporal proximity (Rashid et al., 2016). A schematic illustration of how this mechanism is implemented on the engram level is depicted in Fig. 3. The Trace Consolidation and Trace Competition accounts are the most prominent explanations of the wakeful rest effect. However, their proposed mechanisms might not be the only contributing factors. Rehearsal opportunity and working memory availability present obvious confounds, as during the wakeful rest condition, participants are free to think about or rehearse the memory material, allowing the representation to remain in working memory. This has been addressed by probing participants' thought content during the delay interval and excluding participants reporting rehearsal (e.g., Varma et al., 2018), by employing washout periods prior to retrieval in which task engagement prohibits prolonged working memory maintenance (e.g., Dewar et al., 2014), by using material that is inherently difficult to rehearse, like abstract shapes (e.g., Millar & Balota, 2022), and by obscuring later retrieval by relying on incidental encoding paradigms (e.g., Leetham et al., 2024). As wakeful rest effects are observed in studies employing these methods, rehearsal is thought to play at most a minor role in the overall wakeful rest effect.

A further possible confound of the wakeful rest effect lies in participants falling asleep more easily in the wakeful rest condition than in the comparator condition, which could contribute to the effect via the initiation of sleep-specific consolidation processes (Walker & Stickgold, 2004). Again, the wakeful rest effect is observed in studies excluding participants in which potential sleep was observed or reported (Humiston & Wamsley, 2018). Additionally, the wakeful rest effect seems to be especially pronounced in the first few minutes following encoding (e.g., Dewar et al., 2009). In light of these findings, substantial contributions of sleep to the wakeful rest effect seem unlikely (see also Wamsley, 2022), but cannot be fully ruled out as microsleep and transitions into early sleep stages could occur (Hertig-Godeschalk et al., 2020). Retrieval state represents another possible confound, as it likely differs between wakeful rest and comparator conditions. It is plausible that participants are more relaxed, rested, and less fatigued following the wakeful rest conditions, which might impact retrieval (see e.g., Nava et al., 2004). Another possible benefit of using washout periods before retrieval is in allowing similar retrieval states for both wakeful rest and comparator conditions, which makes substantial contributions of performance differences at retrieval a less plausible driver of wakeful rest effects (e.g., Dewar et al., 2014).

Despite the wakeful rest effect being commonly observed, its magnitude varies substantially between studies, with some researchers observing substantial benefits following rest (e.g., Cowan et al., 2004) and some failing to replicate the effect (e.g., Varma et al., 2019). A plausible reason for the heterogeneity in results, besides measurement error, lies in differing methodologies across studies. As such, the relationship between wakeful rest effect magnitude and specific experimental characteristics can provide insights into the mechanisms underlying the effect. In fact, despite sharing a core paradigm, wakeful rest studies vary substantially, for instance, regarding duration of the delay interval, task(s) during the comparator condition, memory material, memory measure, experimental design, and study population. This leads to two main issues in trying to understand the wakeful rest effect. First, these variations across multiple factors make it difficult to directly compare individual wakeful rest studies and identify important moderators of the effect. Second, individual studies directly investigating the impact of single moderators have limited generalizability, as they realistically have to keep other potential moderators relating to experimental design constant to restrict study complexity to feasible levels. By aggregating data from multiple studies, it is possible to generalize the moderation effects of experimental characteristics on the wakeful rest effect across diverse experimental conditions. Additionally, aggregating data from multiple studies allows for testing moderation effects even in the absence of individual studies directly testing those effects.

Three previous investigations have used meta-analytic approaches to estimate an aggregate wakeful rest effect based on studies published up to 2024. Humiston et al. (2019) contextualized the results of their own experimental study by conducting a meta-analysis including theirs and eleven closely matched studies investigating the wakeful rest effect for verbal material in healthy adults. They estimated an aggregate wakeful rest effect of d = 0.38. Weng et al. (2025) took a more exhaustive approach, including 36 peer-reviewed wakeful rest studies published until April 2024 using varying designs in healthy humans. Additionally, they investigated several important moderators and, for instance, found larger wakeful rest effects for older than for younger adults. They did, however, not include the comparator condition in their moderator analysis. The aggregate wakeful rest effect was estimated as g = 0.45 in this meta-analysis. Parra et al. (2026) added to the previous attempts mainly by quantitatively investigating the impact of comparator conditions and considering memory-impaired populations, who showed particularly large wakeful rest effects. They estimated a slightly smaller aggregate wakeful rest effect of g = 0.34 from a comparable pool of studies as Weng et al. (2025), by including 43 peer-reviewed studies and 8 other records published until May 2024.

With this review and meta-analysis, we aim to update and expand on this previous work by taking a critical look at the mechanisms that have been proposed to underlie the wakeful rest effect and by evaluating their applicability based on the available behavioral as well as neurophysiological data. By using meta-analytic methods and thoroughly reviewing relevant literature, we hope to contribute to a deeper theory-driven understanding of the wakeful rest effect specifically and the impact of post-encoding activity on memory performance generally. In doing so, we pose the following questions: 1) What is the magnitude of the wakeful rest effect?

2) How universal is the wakeful rest effect, i.e., how much does it depend on specific experimental characteristics and study population? 3) What can wakeful rest studies tell us about the memory mechanisms underlying the effect?

2 Methods

2.1 Preregistration

Reporting of the review follows the PRISMA guidelines (Liberati et al., 2009). See Appendix F for a checklist. A detailed study protocol was preregistered with PROSPERO (CRD42023487595).

2.2 Eligibility Criteria

This review included English or German-language peer-reviewed studies comparing declarative memory performance of humans after delay intervals containing either wakeful rest or some form of interference-inducing task. Eligibility of studies was assessed based on their accordance with prespecified criteria using the PICOT framework (Haynes, 2006). To be eligible, studies needed to P) include either healthy or memory-impaired (as defined via clinical assessment or psychometric testing) adult human participants, I) administer a period of wakeful rest following the presentation of memory material, C) administer a period of interference-inducing activity following the presentation of memory material, O) report declarative memory performance, and T) refer to the first retrieval of memory material following the intervention.

2.3 Search Strategy

An initial search string was developed based on the relevant studies identified prior to the systematic search. This initial search string was used to query a list of databases and iteratively adapted based on its performance. Criteria for performance were sensitivity and specificity regarding a list of previously known target studies. This procedure was largely implemented using the R package litsearchr (Grames et al., 2019).

The general iterative process, and specifically record handling and search result evaluation, were aided by CiteSource (Riley et al., 2024). The search string was adapted for the specific databases it was used to query and used for the following databases and search engines : PsycInfo, PsycAbstracts, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar.

The search focused on search terms within the titles, abstracts, and keywords of the records within the databases. Due to the search string and query constraints of Google Scholar, a different search string was used to query it (see Appendix B), and search results were extracted using Harzing's Publish or Perish software (version 8.16; Harzing, 2007). Database queries were conducted on 21.06.2024 (for Google Scholar) and 20.06.2024 (for the other databases). Updated queries were conducted on 20.05.2026 and 29.09.2026. The applied search strings and a detailed breakdown of the records extracted from different databases can be found in Appendix B.

2.4 Study Selection

Search results were exported and merged, as well as deduplicated using CiteSource (Riley et al., 2024). The resulting bibliography was then uploaded to Covidence (Covidence systematic review software, 2025), where a second automatic deduplication was run. Study titles and abstracts were then screened for eligibility by author WP and either DB or PL. Eligibility conflicts were resolved by rater agreement following discussion. Another round of eligibility screening was conducted based on the full text of the records identified during abstract screening, with the same procedure for conflict resolution. Reasons for exclusion from the second round of eligibility screening were recorded and are presented in the PRISMA flow diagram in Fig. 4 2.5 Data Extraction Authors WP and PL extracted and coded information from the final list of eligible studies. The WebPlotDigitizer (version 4.6; Rohatgi, 2022) was used to extract data from studies in which critical information was not reported in text but could be extracted from figures.

In case information necessary for eligibility judgments, statistics to calculate effect sizes, or other relevant study characteristics were missing and not recoverable otherwise, we attempted to contact the respective corresponding authors of the studies and asked them to provide the missing information. When the corresponding authors did not comply with our request, the respective study was excluded from the review (see Appendix B for studies excluded due to missing information and study author non-response).

The main outcome of interest was declarative memory performance following the intervention. Accordingly, all such measures (mean and standard deviation) were extracted or calculated from the included studies. In case multiple measures of memory performance (e.g., proportion recalled and number of items recognized) were provided, all such measures were extracted. If there were multiple measures within a single study, e.g., one measure immediately following the intervention and another measure seven days later, both outcomes were extracted for further investigation. Since only two eligible studies reported EEG results (Brokaw et al., 2016; Scalia & Wamsley, 2025), EEG outcomes were not extracted for further synthesis or analysis.

Outside the main outcome of declarative memory performance following the intervention, we extracted and coded: basic study information (titles, publication years, journals, authors, researcher affiliations; demographics of the study sample (age, sex or gender, population); and methodological study parameters (type of interference condition, type of memory measure, type of memory material, modality of memory material presentation, duration of intervention, time between encoding and delayed retrieval). Additional study information was extracted but not analyzed; this information can be found in the provided data.

2.6 Risk of bias

Risk of bias (RoB) for each of the included studies was assessed independently by WP and PL using criteria provided in the RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019). Conflicting risk of bias assessments were resolved via discussion. As both within-and between-group design studies were included, different RoB tools were used, namely the RoB 2 tool for crossover trials for within-design studies and the RoB 2 tool for between-design studies (Sterne et al., 2019).

2.7 Statistical Analyses 2.7.1 Software R (version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2023) and primarily the metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010) package were used to conduct the meta-analyses and related analyses. All code and data used to conduct the analyses presented in the following can be found in the Open Science Framework (OSF) repository accompanying this paper.

2.7.2 Summary effect size

Standardized mean differences were extracted or calculated based on information found in the selected records. Effect sizes were calculated as Hedges' gav and Hedges' gs for within-and between-group differences, respectively, based on recommendations by Lakens (2013). Exact formulas are provided in Appendix A. Positive effect sizes represent better memory performance in the wakeful rest condition compared to a comparator condition.

2.7.3 Meta-Analysis & moderator analyses

Most of the meta-analytic framework described in the following was adapted from Liu et al. (2025). As several studies provide multiple effects, the individual effects we aimed to aggregate are highly dependent. These effects are expressed across different memory measures; they are also nested in samples, which in turn are nested in studies. To account for dependency among effects on different levels, we initially created a cross-classified random effects meta-regression model (CCREM) with four levels (Fernández-Castilla et al., 2019). This relatively complex model served as our starting point for a backward model selection approach, in which we compared successively less complex models with our starting model by removing random effects and conducting likelihood ratio tests comparing the models. In case the simple model fit the data equally well or better than the complex model, we continued with the simpler model; otherwise, we retained the complex model. To constrain the search space, we compared candidate models representing the most sensible iterative reduction in complexity based on our prior assumptions regarding possible clustering of the data.

2.7.4 Sample heterogeneity

Heterogeneity was tested using a Q test, and I² and τ² measures of heterogeneity were calculated.

Observed I² values were interpreted based on conventional standards, with I² values between 30% and 60%, 50% to 90%, and 75% to 100% being interpreted as evidence for moderate, substantial, and considerable heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al., 2019).

2.7.5 Moderator variables

To investigate the influence of moderators on the wakeful rest effect, we extended the multilevel meta-regression framework used for the overall effect calculation by adding individual moderators as predictors to the model. Moderator levels with fewer than five contributing effects were omitted from analysis. Following significant omnibus tests of moderation, post-hoc comparisons of the resulting estimates were used to examine the differences across categorical moderator levels. Holm correction (Holm, 1979) was used to correct for multiple comparisons. The continuous moderators, age, manipulation duration, and year of publication, were investigated using the same framework by adding the moderators as continuous variables without further recoding. Based on the number of individually significant moderators and their potential association, additional exploratory analyses regarding moderator overlap were conducted and are presented in Appendix H.

2.7.6 Outliers and influential cases

In order to determine the robustness of the meta-analysis results and their dependence on singular studies and effects, leave-one-out (LOO) sensitivity analyses were conducted for individual effects, unique samples, and studies. Outlier effects were identified based on studentized residuals (Viechtbauer & Cheung, 2010) and Cook's distance (Cook & Weisberg, 1982) of individual contributing effects. A summary effect that excluded effects marked as outliers was calculated.

2.8 Data quality, small study bias, and power

To investigate small study bias, an Egger's regression test (Egger et al., 1997) was performed. Additionally, a contour-enhanced funnel plot was used to assess small study bias via visual inspection. To correct for small study bias, the precision-effect test-precision-effect estimate with standard error (PET-PEESE) procedure (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014) was used. Using the aggregate effect size of our final synthesis result, the power of individual studies was calculated and visualized using a sunset plot.

3 Results

3.1 Study inclusion

Following full-text screening, we included 59 studies published between 2004 and 2026. Note that each record corresponds to a single unique report and study. Four of these studies had to be excluded as they did not include critical information needed to calculate summary effect sizes, and the respective corresponding authors did not respond when asked to provide the missing information (see Appendix B). From the remaining 55 studies, we extracted 142 contributing effects. 97 unique samples contributed to these effects, consisting of 4005 unique participants (62.52 % female) in total. While most studies report information on sex or gender, it is often unclear which is meant specifically or how it was assessed. The age of the participants was between 18 and 90 (M = 29.90, SDpooled = 5.34). For a breakdown of the number of contributing effects and unique participants, see Fig. 7.

3.2 Risk of bias

Risk of bias was assessed at the level of studies. 47 out of 55 studies show low risk of bias, 8 out of 55 show some concern, and no studies show a high level of concern. RoB assessments for individual records can be found in Appendix D. The most common reason for concern was the lack of reported blinding regarding condition in studies employing memory performance measures potentially affected by bias (e.g., free recall of previously told stories).

3.3 Individual study results

The individual effects extracted ranged from -0.83 to 2.87, with a median effect size of g = 0.33. The power of the studies ranged from 6.50 % to 96.24%, with a median power of 41.91%. An overview of individual effects contributing to the meta-analysis can be found in Fig. 5 and Appendix G.

3.4 Synthesis

According to the adopted model selection approach, a three-level meta-analysis performed the best (see Appendix C for an overview of the compared candidate models). The chosen model includes the sampling variance of each effect size (Level 1), the variance between effects within the same study (Level 2), and the variance between studies (Level 3). The resulting aggregate effect size of the wakeful rest effect was g = 0.35 (95% CI [0.23, 0.46], p < .001).

There was considerable heterogeneity between the contributing effects, Q(141) = 567.03, p < .001. The estimated variance components were τ² Level3 = 0.14 (95% CI [0.07, 0.24]) and τ² Level2 = 0.04 (95% CI [0.02, 0.08]). I² Level3 = 62.60% of the total variation can be attributed to betweenstudy heterogeneity, and I² Level2 = 20.17% to within-study heterogeneity. Profile plots displaying the likelihood of variance components can be found in Appendix C.

3.5 Sensitivity & Outlier Analysis

Seven influential outliers were identified based on both Cook's distance and studentized residuals criteria. See a list of the identified outliers in Appendix C. Excluding these outliers yielded an aggregated effect size slightly smaller than the original analysis including those outliers, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.21, 0.41], p < .001.

Additionally, we conducted leave-one-out analyses at the level of individual effect sizes, unique samples, and studies. For the leave-one-out analysis of individual effects, the minimum observed effect size was g = 0.34, 95% CI [0.22, 0.45], p < .001, and the maximum g = 0.36, 95% CI [0.24, 0.48], p < .001. For the leave-one-out analysis of unique samples, the minimum observed effect size was g = 0.34, 95% CI [0.22, 0.45], p < .001, and the maximum g = 0.36, 95% CI [0.24, 0.48], p < .001. For the leave-one-out analysis of studies, the minimum observed effect size was g = 0.33, 95% CI [0.22, 0.44], p < 0.001, and the maximum g = 0.36, 95% CI [0.25, 0.48], p < .001.

Further, the meta-analysis was recalculated using robust variance estimation (RVE), resulting in an overall effect size similar to the original three-level meta-analysis model (g = 0.35, 95% CI [0.23, 0.47], p < .001). See Fig. 6 for an overview of aggregate effects using different correction methods.

Fig. 6. Overview of sensitivity and robustness analyses. Shown is the original aggregate effect in comparison to various other estimates of an aggregate effect, including leave-one-out (LOO) analyses on the levels of study, sample, and effect, robust variance estimate (RVE), and precision-effect estimate with standard error (PEESE). The dotted lines show the mean and upper and lower bounds of the 95 % confidence interval of the original three-level model.

3.6 Moderators 3.6.1 Population

There was a significant moderation of population on the wakeful rest effect, F(2,139) = 20.01, p < .001. Post-hoc comparisons revealed significant differences between younger healthy adults (g = 0.25, 95% CI [0.14, 0.35]) and healthy older adults (g = 0.53, 95% CI [0.36, 0.69]), p = .004, as well as memory-impaired patients (g = 0.82, 95% CI [0.56, 1.08]), p < .001. The difference between healthy older adults and memory-impaired patients was also significant, p = .03.

Additionally, across all included effects, mean sample age moderated the wakeful rest effect, B1 = 0.009 (95% CI [0.005, 0.012]), t(135) = 4.52, p < .001. For a visualization of moderation effects, see Fig. 7.

3.6.2 Comparator

There was a significant moderation of the comparator condition on the wakeful rest effect, F(4,137) = 19.40, p < .001. Post-hoc comparisons revealed significant differences between tests, learning and retrieval tasks (g = 0.58, 95% CI [0.37, 0.79]) and attention and working memory tasks (g = 0.17, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.34]), p = .022, as well as video games (g = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.36, 0.31]), p = .027. Post-hoc comparisons also revealed significant differences between visual identification tasks (g = 0.47, 95% CI [0.32, 0.61]) and attention and working memory tasks (g = 0.17, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.34]), p = .030. Post-hoc comparisons between other comparator conditions were not significant.

3.6.3 Memory Measure

There was a significant moderation of memory measure on the wakeful rest effect, F(1,140) = 5.82, p = .016. Post-hoc comparisons revealed significantly greater effects for recall (g = 0.40, 95% CI [0.28, 0.52]) than for recognition measures (g = 0.22, 95% CI [0.07, 0.37]), p = .016.

3.6.4 Modality

There was a significant moderation of modality on the wakeful rest effect, F(2,139) = 10.52, p = .005. Post-hoc comparisons revealed a significant difference between auditory (g = 0.52, 95% CI [0.37, 0.67]) and visual (g = 0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35]) presentation, p = .004. Post-hoc comparisons between audiovisual presentation and other modalities were not significant.

3.6.5 Material

There was no significant moderation of memory material on the wakeful rest effect, F(1,140) = 3.62, p = .057.

3.6.6 Duration

There was no significant moderation of manipulation duration on the wakeful rest effect, B1 = 0.0001 (95% CI [-0.0001, 0.0002]), t(140) = 0.73, p = .469.

3.6.7 Delay

There was no significant moderation of delay between encoding and first delayed retrieval on the wakeful rest effect, F(2,137) = 0.26, p = .880.

3.6.8 Design Factors

There was no significant moderation of the use of within-or between-design on the wakeful rest effect, F(1,140) = 0.26, p = .612. There was no significant moderation of encoding instruction on the wakeful rest effect, F(1,140) = 1.10, p = .293. There was no significant moderation of immediate retrieval on the wakeful rest effect, F(1,140) = 0.24, p = .624. There was no significant moderation of washout periods on the wakeful rest effect, F(1,140) = 0.010, p = .917.

3.6.9 Meta Factors

There was a significant moderation of publication year on the wakeful rest effect, B1 = -0.05 (95% CI [-0.07, -0.03]), t(140) = -5.54, p < .001. There was also a significant moderation of researcher affiliation on the wakeful rest effect, F(4,137) = 32.96, p < 0.001. Post-hoc comparisons revealed significantly larger effects for studies conducted by the Edinburgh group (UE) (g = 0.67, 95% CI immediate retrieval, dark gray = presence of a washout period, light gray = delay between encoding and first delayed retrieval).

3.7 Publication Bias

Both visual inspection of the funnel plot (see Fig. 8) and Egger's regression test B1 = 3.07, 95% CI [2.21, 3.93], SE = 0.44, p < .001 indicate substantial small-study bias. After controlling for the standard error of the effect size, the intercept of this regression was significantly different from zero, B0 = -0.35, 95% CI [-0.56, -0.13], SE = 0.11, p < .001. Therefore, the precision-effect estimate with standard error (PEESE) method was used to correct for small-study bias because the true underlying effect is likely not zero (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014). After PEESE correction, the observed overall effect size was reduced to g = 0.05, with a 95% CI ranging from -0.07 to 0.17, p = .428. Statistical power of included effects, as visualized in the sunset plot in Fig. 8, reveals low statistical power in most effects, and the median power of all included effects was 41.91%.

4 Discussion

4.1 Summary and general effect

Our results show a moderate benefit of wakeful rest on memory performance of g = 0.35 (95% CI [0.23, 0.47]), although there is considerable heterogeneity across included studies and evidence of small-study bias. Overall, this estimate is in line with previous estimates (Humiston et al., 2019; Weng et al., 2025; Parra et al., 2026), yet it is the result of the synthesis of 12 more peer-reviewed studies than the last meta-analytic approach (Parra et al., 2026)While this benefit is general, it is not universal as it depends on specific experimental conditions and study sample, with aggregate effect estimates ranging from substantial (g = 0.82, 95% CI [0.56, 1.08]) to null (g = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.36, 0.31]) depending on the presence of specific study features (see Fig. 7).

Finding out which study features are especially relevant allows us to better understand how the wakeful rest effect comes to be.

4.2 Moderation of wakeful rest effects 4.2.1 Comparator condition

The wakeful rest effect represents a differential measure in that it compares memory performance following two different post-encoding conditions. As such, it is inherently dependent on the chosen reference, i.e., the comparator condition. Our results indicate an overall moderation of the comparator condition on wakeful rest effect magnitude. Specifically, the aggregate data show the largest wakeful rest effects when the comparator presented demand on the memory system via psychological tests, learning, and retrieval as well as spot-the-difference and visual identification tasks, and the smallest effects for video games and attentional or working memory tasks. This is consistent with direct experimental evidence (e.g., Craig et al., 2014; Varma et al., 2018) and the theoretical assumptions of both the Trace Consolidation and Competition accounts, implicating encoding and retrieval demands over general cognitive engagement in causing interference and, in turn, driving the wakeful rest effect.

Despite an alignment between theoretical assumptions, direct experimental results, and the aggregate data, several individual experimental results are inconsistent with this notion. In one case, Martini et al. (2020) find no wakeful rest effect in a study using a comparator condition in which participants were asked to read and remember a newspaper article, which should imply considerable encoding demand. Additionally, Dewar et al. (2007) find substantial wakeful rest benefits when using a simple tone detection task as a comparator condition, which presents little if any apparent demand on the memory system. To clarify the reliance of the wakeful rest effect on the cognitive demands presented by the comparator, additional research is needed in which encoding and retrieval demands are directly manipulated and specified more clearly.

4.2.2 Population & Age

Our results show larger wakeful rest effect magnitudes in memory-impaired and healthy older samples compared with healthy younger samples. addition, memory-impaired samples show larger wakeful rest effects than healthy older samples, which is consistent with individual study results (e.g., Alber et al., 2014). As memory performance generally declines with age (e.g., Cansino, 2009), we can tentatively relate wakeful rest effect magnitude to overall memory capabilities, and larger wakeful rest effects are related to worse a priori memory performance. While the aggregate data support this interpretation, which was also reached by Parra et al. (2026), the substantial heterogeneity in results for memory-impaired samples warrants a more nuanced consideration of the individual studies.

Large wakeful rest effects have been observed in patients with varying pathologies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), (amnestic) mild cognitive impairment (aMCI, MCI), head injuries, stroke, anoxia, hypoxia, encephalitis and obstructive hydrocephalus (Alber et al., 2014; Cowan et al., 2004; Della Salla et al., 2005; Dewar et al., 2010; McGhee et al., 2020). Some of these pathologies are closely linked to hippocampal and medial temporal lobe integrity, while others are relatively unrelated. In fact, several studies find evidence of reduced wakeful rest benefits for patients exhibiting hippocampus involvement.

Cowan et al. (2004) see no wakeful rest benefit for the temporal lobe lesion patients included in their study. Della Salla et al. (2005) report null effects for a pilot sample of AD patients, while showing clear benefits for MCI patients. Fittingly, Dewar et al. (2012) find reduced wakeful rest benefits for AD compared to aMCI patients. Finally, Sandry et al. ( 2019) report null effects for memory-impaired multiple sclerosis patients, for whom hippocampal involvement is common (Ontaneda et al., 2021; Rocca et al., 2018). This pattern of results suggests that in profound anterograde amnesia linked to hippocampal damage, the relation between memory impairment and the benefit of wakeful rest breaks down.

Such a relationship between wakeful rest effect magnitude and hippocampal integrity has clear implications for the roles of trace competition and consolidation. Under the Trace Competition account, we would expect hippocampal damage to be associated with an even greater vulnerability to retroactive interference and, in turn, greater wakeful rest effects, as the hippocampus is not only critically relevant for encoding but also for retrieval (Yassa & Reagh, 2013). In contrast, under the Trace Consolidation account, a core function linked to the hippocampus lies in orchestrating consolidation mechanisms (Squire et al., 2015). Accordingly, substantial damage to the hippocampus disrupts consolidation and thus should reduce wakeful rest effects, which are thought to be a result of facilitated consolidation. This is consistent with recent neuroscientific findings by Shipley et al. (2026), who showed that AD model mice exhibit distinct memory deficits in a radial arm maze task. These deficits were accompanied by degraded replay and reduced plasticity during offline periods following learning, which corresponds to a smaller benefit of rest compared to their wild-type counterparts. Taken together, while the exact relation between neuropathology and wakeful rest effect magnitude remains obscure, converging evidence points to 1) stronger wakeful rest effects in aging and some forms of memory impairment and 2) a dependency of the wakeful rest effect on the hippocampus and consolidation mechanisms enabled by it.

4.2.3 Memory Measure

Our results indicate larger wakeful rest effects for recall than for recognition. This could be a result of facilitated retrieval in recognition tasks. Retrieval cues provided during recognition tasks can aid in trace reinstatement needed for the retrieval of relevant memory traces (Danker & Anderson, 2010; Rau et al., 2026). As such, facilitated reinstatement during retrieval in recognition tasks alone could protect memory traces from retroactive interference. Critically, this is the case for retroactive interference resulting in both insufficient and ambiguous reinstatement corresponding to the Trace Consolidation and Trace Competition accounts, respectively.

4.2.4 Memory Modality and Material

The wakeful rest effect magnitude is associated with the sensory modality in which the memory material was presented. Auditory presentation leads to larger effects than visual presentation. Additionally, there is a trend of verbal material being associated with larger wakeful rest effects than other material. This trend is of note as modality is strongly linked to material, with nearly all studies presenting memory material aurally also using verbal material. This makes it difficult to disentangle modality and material clearly. Nevertheless, based on this pattern, we speculate that wakeful rest effects increase when remembering is particularly difficult, possibly due to weaker encoding of the relevant memory traces. Regarding modality, auditory presentation is often brief and strictly paced, which can lead to weakened encoding. Supporting this idea, Fatania & Mercer (2017) showed that simply increasing encoding time can reduce wakeful rest effects in children. It is also possible that auditory presentation evokes representation of the memory trace in a short-term sensory store (Baddeley & Hitch, 2019), which fits observations of more pronounced recency effects for auditory material (Glenberg, 1984). This sensory storage is likely particularly vulnerable to interference and, in turn, benefits from reduced interference during wakeful rest. Regarding memory material, pictures can be easier to remember than words for the same content, which has been called the picture superiority effect (Paivio et al., 1968). This effect has been linked to more elaborate semantic processing and potentially stronger encoding of pictures than words (Hockley, 2008).

4.2.5 Duration

Duration of the delay period, i.e., length of the rest and comparator condition, did not moderate wakeful rest effect magnitude. This is in line with the idea of a temporal gradient of retroactive interference and interference affecting memory performance more strongly if it occurs closer to encoding (as reviewed by Wixted, 2004). Accordingly, the first seconds to minutes following encoding seem to be crucial for later retrieval, and even short delay periods can produce large wakeful rest effects. Ultimately, both the Trace Consolidation account and Trace Competition account address this temporal gradient with the assumption of early trace instability, i.e., vulnerability to interference (Dewar et al., 2009) and reduced temporal distinctiveness of traces, respectively (Ecker et al., 2015a).

4.2.6 Stability

Memory benefits following brief periods of post-encoding wakeful rest have been observed to be present up to seven days after encoding (e.g., Alber et al., 2014), with anecdotal observations of patients with severe anterograde amnesia remembering information tangential to study participation even a year after encoding (Dewar et al., 2010). In line with these individual observations, our results indicate that, across studies included in our meta-analysis, the magnitude of the wakeful rest effect does not diminish with longer delays between the postencoding phase and delayed retrieval. The stability of the wakeful rest effect shows a lasting change in the retrieval probability of the memory traces, aligning with both the Trace Consolidation and Trace Competition accounts. While memory performance can be improved both in a context-dependent and a general manner by relaxation during retrieval (Cassaday et al., 2002), our aggregate results, in addition to prior findings, oppose the idea that wakeful rest effects depend on retrieval state.

4.2.7 Design Factors

Between-group design, washout periods, intent of remembering, and immediate retrieval constitute theoretically important facets of experimental design. However, none of the design factors considered here were found to moderate the wakeful rest effect magnitude. Employment of these measures is thought to lessen the potential impact of rehearsal on the wakeful rest effect (see also Wamsley, 2022). Between-group design (e.g., Dewar et al., 2014), immediate retrieval (e.g., Dewar et al., 2009), and incidental encoding paradigms (e.g., Leetham et al., 2024) obfuscate the presence of a delayed retrieval phase and reduce participants' motivation to rehearse memory material during the delay period. A washout period can prevent rehearsal prior to retrieval (e.g., Dewar et al., 2014). In addition to observations of wakeful rest effects when probing participants' thought content during the delay period and excluding participants reporting rehearsal (e.g., Varma et al., 2018), this offers considerable evidence of the wakeful rest effect being largely independent of conscious rehearsal processes. Instead, the wakeful rest effect is likely a product of automatic and unconscious mechanisms, which aligns with both the Trace Consolidation and Competition accounts.

4.2.8 Meta Factors

We see clear moderation effects of both researcher affiliation and year of publication. Larger effects are observed in the earliest studies included in this review, as well as studies conducted by the UE group and affiliated researchers. Additionally, we observe substantial small-study bias and low power of most of the included studies. All of these findings may, at a surface level, appear problematic and might be indicative of issues relating to the scientific process. However, the UE group contributed the majority of early studies investigating the phenomenon (Cowan et al., 2004; Della Sala et al., 2005; Dewar et al., 2007). Also, many of their studies investigate memory-impaired populations Cowan et al., 2004; Della Sala et al., 2005; Dewar et al., 2009; Dewar et al., 2010; Dewar et al., 2012; Alber et al., 2014), which plausibly explains both the large effects and small sample sizes. Additionally, the UE group employs spot-the-difference tasks as comparator conditions more often than other groups (e.g., Dewar et al., 2012), and spotthe-difference tasks are also related to larger wakeful rest effects.

Due to the correlational nature of the aggregate data, undocumented idiosyncrasies in the work of specific researchers or research groups, inflating the wakeful rest effect estimates, cannot be ruled out. However, investigating methodological quality and assessing the risk of bias of individual studies indicates no systematic issues with studies produced by any group of researchers. Ultimately, experimental specifications, namely use of older or memory-impaired samples and visual identification comparator conditions, in addition to measurement error, present plausible explanations for the present results. Thus, the evolution of individual study effect magnitudes over time can be understood as an "under-specified decline effect" (Protzko & Schooler, 2017). The striking results of PEESE correction, which show a substantial attenuation of the estimated effect size under the assumption of small-study bias towards null, are contextualized by the previously discussed pattern of findings. While there is considerable numerical evidence of small-study bias in the data, this is plausibly a consequence of actual moderators of wakeful rest effect magnitude being associated with sample size. For example, included studies of memory-impaired populations generally have smaller samples and larger effects than included studies of healthy younger adults. In addition, PET-PEESE procedures perform poorly under high heterogeneity (Stanley, 2017), which is present in the data. Based on these considerations, we decided to base our interpretation on the original uncorrected effect, which according to the other sensitivity analyses performed, is robust.

4.3 Strengths, Limitations, and Outlook

This review and meta-analysis aggregates the empirical findings of the wakeful rest effect and relates the results of this extensive synthesis with the results of prior studies on memory on a behavioral and neurobiological level. In doing so, it provides both a broad overview of the wakeful rest effect and a narrow discussion of the underlying memory mechanisms. By considering 12 more peer-reviewed studies than the largest previous meta-analysis (Parra et al., 2026), this review additionally provides a needed update and expansion to prior work and, as such, a more comprehensive overview of the field.

As discussed above, substantial small-study bias combined with the inadequate power of most included studies points to systematic issues within this field of research that might affect the synthesized results. By taking the results of our moderator analyses into account, effect size estimation and, with it, sample size calculation of future studies on the wakeful rest effect can be improved to address these issues. Another limitation of many meta-analytic approaches, which is especially relevant here, is the dependency between factors of experimental design in the contributing studies. As an example, the FU group is the only group of researchers using video games as comparator conditions (e.g., Brokaw et al., 2016), and they are exclusively investigating younger adults across the included studies. The UE group, on the other hand, tends to use spot-the-difference comparators and often investigates older or memory-impaired adults (e.g., Alber et al., 2014). Dependencies like these between the research group, the comparator condition, and the sample of interest limit the conclusions that can be drawn by aggregating the data.

While meta-analysis is a powerful tool to gain a broad understanding of the wakeful rest effect and to tentatively fill gaps in our understanding, it cannot replace data from experiments in isolating the influence of specific experimental conditions. The need for additional experimental data is especially pronounced when addressing questions regarding the underlying neural mechanisms behind the wakeful rest effect. To date, there are only two studies relating electrophysiological results to the wakeful rest effect (Brokaw et al., 2016; Scalia & Wamsley, 2026). Despite our initial plans, we could therefore not collate the available studies to gain further insights into the relations between electrophysiology and behavior. Most importantly, consolidation-related mechanisms like memory reactivation and replay have not yet been investigated in relation to wakeful rest effects, which presents a fundamental gap to be filled by future research.

4.4 Conclusion

In conclusion, the aggregate data show that short periods of wakeful rest following encoding benefit memory performance in humans. While this is generally true, the magnitude of the effect critically depends on the experimental conditions under which it is observed. In particular, wakeful rest benefits are increased 1) when rest is compared to comparator conditions heavily taxing our memory system with encoding and/or retrieval demands, 2) when the memory material itself is especially difficult to remember, e.g., when it is initially presented only auditorily, briefly, and has to be freely recalled, and 3) when overall a priori memory performance is reduced, as it is in aging and memory impairment. At the same time, human memory is remarkably resilient to interference due to post-encoding activity, which allows us to adaptively function and learn in a world filled with potentially interfering distractions.

Regarding the neurobiological mechanisms behind the wakeful rest effect, it remains unclear to what degree the effect is a consequence of facilitated consolidation or reduced competition of memory traces. Contrary to the dominant view of wakeful rest being primarily a consequence of facilitated consolidation, our data are largely aligned with both the Trace Consolidation and the Trace Competition accounts. It is likely that both facilitated trace consolidation and reduced trace competition contribute to the overall wakeful rest effect, and their relative contributions depend on the specific conditions under which the effect is observed.

Fig 7. Forest plot of aggregate wakeful rest effect sizes (wakeful rest -comparator conditions). Each effect represents the aggregate effect of all the effects with the respective study feature present. n indicates the number of individual participants contributing to the aggregate effect, and k indicates the number of unique samples contributing to the aggregate effect. Effects are grouped and color-coded by the overarching moderator analysis, with gray indicating nonsignificant moderation effects (from top to bottom: orange = study population, light blue = comparator, green = memory measure, pink = modality of memory material, dark gray = type of memory material, light gray = design, dark gray = encoding instruction, light gray = presence of

Fig 8.

Fig 8. Sunset funnel plot. White dots represent individual contributing effects. The vertical black line represents the aggregate wakeful rest effect. This effect was used for power analysis. The shaded dark areas represent significance contours at p = 0.05 and 0.01. The dashed blue line represents the fit line from the Egger's regression test model.
